entities.name: Einsiedeln Abbey
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Einsiedeln Abbey (Kloster Einsiedeln) in Switzerland, founded in 934 on the site of hermit Meinrad's 9th-century cell, is one of the most important pilgrimage destinations in Europe and the largest Benedictine monastery in Switzerland. The Black Madonna of Einsiedeln — a 15th-century statue of Mary as a black-faced figure — has drawn pilgrims for over 1,000 years; approximately 200,000 pilgrims per year make Einsiedeln the most visited pilgrimage site in the German-speaking world.

Meinrad, a monk from Reichenau who sought solitude in the forest of Einsiedeln, was killed by robbers in 861. His hermitage became a pilgrimage site; the Benedictine abbey was formally established in 934. The Black Madonna's history includes multiple catastrophes — the abbey was burned by French Revolutionary troops in 1798, and the statue hidden — but rebuilt and restored. The statue's dark complexion (from centuries of candle smoke) has made it an object of special veneration as one of Europe's Black Madonnas.

Einsiedeln's library, with over 200,000 volumes and 1,000 medieval manuscripts, is one of Switzerland's most important cultural collections. The abbey school, one of Switzerland's oldest, educated playwright and mystic Paracelsus and continues today. Einsiedeln's Baroque architecture (1704-1735) by Caspar Moosbrugger is considered the finest example of Central European Baroque religious architecture.
